idiom_name: one-line delegating method with an intention-revealing selector
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: pick the operation callers repeat, name it after the intent rather than the mechanism, and implement it as exactly one message send to the delegate on a single line (cancel_order(order_id) -> delegate.cancel(order_id)). Keep the delegate injected rather than created inside the body so the method stays substitutable and testable, and keep the member non-virtual where the language allows it so the extra hop can be inlined away. Delete the method the moment its name stops adding information: a forwarder that only restates the delegate's selector is the Middle Man smell, not this pattern.
code_sketch:
# caller (reads as intent)
service.cancel_order(order_id)

# the one-line delegating method
cancel_order(order_id):
    return repo.cancel(order_id)     # one message send, one line
pitfalls: Skipping the naming test: if the selector says no more than the delegate's own name, the method costs a hop and returns nothing.
Building the delegate inside the body (new/lookup), which makes the one-liner untestable and hides a second responsibility in a method that claims to be one line.
Chaining one-liners so that one operation must be traced through three hops before the code that actually runs is found.

Bulk delegation that erases names: __getattr__, Proxy, or equivalent meta-programming forwards every member without individual names, losing the one-name-per-operation seam that makes override, mock and documentation possible.

Forwarding across a type boundary (e.g. a remote proxy, an async wrapper) where the forwarded call's failure modes differ from the wrapper's contract, so callers that read intent get unexpected latency or error shapes.

Renaming the delegate's method without updating every forwarding selector that calls it, because the forwarder is a different method with its own name that is not mechanically linked to the delegate's.

Wrong move: treat a Go net/http Client call as a cheap local forwarder -> transport errors, redirects, timeouts and body ownership disappear from the wrapper contract -> instead name the remote operation and state its failure and latency semantics at the boundary.

Wrong move: mirror every method of a LoggerAdapter or DelegatingHandler -> the wrapper becomes a Middle Man and callers cannot tell which names add policy -> instead expose only intention-bearing messages whose single send earns the seam.

Wrong move: force a long multi-keyword selector to stay one physical line -> the method becomes harder to review than a normal Composed Method -> instead reduce arity with a Parameter Object or break the message deliberately.
